Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Auditor
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark
  Maladaptive Strategies: Smoking: I smoke, Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
At forty-six, Marcus had spent twenty-three years as an auditor for a regional insurance firm in Honolulu, a career built on predictability, on columns of numbers that always added up, on risk that could be calculated and contained. He had been married to Leilani for nineteen years, and they had two daughters, now grown and living on the mainland. On the first Tuesday of May, three years ago, a flash flood swept through the valley where their home sat. Marcus had been at work. Leilani had been at home. By the time he made it through the rising water to their street, the house was gone, and so was she. He never found her body. The official report listed her as a drowning victim, presumed swept out to sea. What Marcus remembered most vividly, what returned to him in the most unbearable way, was not the water itself but the smell—the thick, wet smell of mud and gasoline and rotting vegetation that had filled the air for weeks afterward. Even now, when he least expected it, that smell would surface. He would be sitting at his desk, reviewing a client’s expense reports, and suddenly the air in the room would change, and he could taste it too, a gritty, metallic tang on his tongue, as though he had just swallowed floodwater. The memory was so extreme, so vivid, that it sometimes felt unreal, like a story that had happened to someone else. But it had happened to him, and he could not stop it from happening again.

The consequences of that morning reshaped every part of his life. He had moved to a small apartment in a high-rise downtown, as far from the valley as he could get while still keeping his job. He told himself it was practical, easier to maintain, closer to the office. But the truth was that he could not bear to be near any physical location that reminded him of the flood—the low-lying roads, the bridges, the stretches of coast where debris had washed up. He stopped driving entirely. He took the bus, always the same route, always the same seat, because unfamiliar places felt impossible. He could not assess the danger in a place he did not know. And so his world had shrunk to a narrow corridor: his apartment, the bus stop, the office, the grocery store two blocks away. He had become an expert at scanning for threat. Silence, for instance, had become unbearable. When the bus was too quiet, or when the hallway outside his apartment was still for too long, his chest would tighten. He was certain that something dangerous was about to happen. He had also noticed that any delay—a bus that was late, a line at the grocery store that moved more slowly than expected—sent a spike of alarm through him. Something bad must be happening. He could not stop bad things from happening to him. That was the belief that had settled into his bones like a low-grade fever.

He had come to believe that relaxing was dangerous. On the rare evenings when he caught himself feeling calm, or when he sat down to watch a movie and felt his shoulders drop, a sharp dread would cut through the ease. He would stand up. He would find something to do. He had started smoking again, a habit he had quit fifteen years ago, because the act of smoking gave his hands and his mouth something to do, and because the ritual felt like a form of vigilance. He did not talk about the flood. When colleagues asked how he was doing, he said he was fine. When his daughters called and tried to get him to talk about their mother, he changed the subject or said he had to go. Talking about it felt like opening a door he had spent three years trying to keep shut. He had no interest in therapy, no interest in support groups. What would be the point? The world was a dangerous place. He knew that now. And he felt dead inside, hollowed out, as though the flood had taken not just his wife but his capacity to feel anything at all.

What finally brought him to seek help was not insight or a crisis. It was a performance review at work. His manager had noted that Marcus seemed distracted, that his usually meticulous reports had begun to contain errors, that he had missed two deadlines in the past quarter. The manager suggested, gently, that he take some leave. Marcus heard the unspoken threat: get help, or your job is at risk. He made an appointment with a psychologist because he was afraid of losing the last predictable thing in his life. He sat in the waiting room with his hands on his knees, breathing through his mouth, trying not to smell anything. He did not know if talking would help. He was almost certain it would not. But he was also tired of living in a world that felt, every moment, like the water was about to rise again.
